newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - T-bond vols dive as calls unloaded.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - T-bond vols dive as calls unloaded.

text.p: U.S. Treasury bond implied volatility plummeted Friday as market participants sold calls in brisk volume as the underlying futures nose-dived.

The heavy call selling in both September and December bond options marked a shift from earlier in the week when mortgage servicers and others were purchasing out-of-the-money calls to hedge against falling interest rates, floor traders said.
September bond futures sank nearly two full points on the day, coming to a halt just off the session low to end down 1-30/32 at 114-26/32.

The price break, triggered by the release of strong U.S. July employment data and upturns in the national purchasing managers' overall and price indexes, followed a series of 1-1/2-year highs in bond futures this week.
The call selling in options helped knock September volatility down a full percentage point, floor brokers said.

The rate bottomed at about 7.40 percent late in the day before clawing back to end at roughly 7.75 percent. December volatility's decline was relatively muted. It dipped to 8.40 percent from 8.65 percent near the opening.

One notable transaction involved unwinding of a huge December call spread established earlier this week, brokers said. The firm today bought 6,000 of the 116-00 strikes and sold 9,000 of the 118-00 strikes. On Wednesday, it was seen selling 20,000 December 116-00 calls and buying 30,000 of the 118-00 calls.
After volatilities had come off, traders also began buying puts and put spreads, floor brokers said. Declining volatility depresses long put positions.
Eurodollar volatilities firmed on the day in contrast to bonds, with December rising 0.7 percentage point to 7.7 percent and March gaining a full point to 11.0 percent.
December Euro futures' 14-basis-point range for the session prompted the bounce in volatility as traders hedged delta exposure, said a Eurodollar broker.
Eurodollar volatilities have been in a year-long slump, so it is too soon to call a bottom, he said.
"Levels should go up, but volatility is not a buy," said the broker. "People will just reassess that the market can move more than four or five basis points at a time."
